transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

I'm here because I've been dealing with really extreme mood swings for over a year now. I alternate between periods of feeling incredibly energetic and irritable, and times when I feel deeply depressed and empty. It has become really hard to manage on my own.

During these periods of extreme mood swings, have you ever experienced any unusual perceptions, such as hearing voices or seeing things that others cannot, or had beliefs that seem unrealistic to others?

No, I've never experienced anything like that. I don't hear or see things that aren't there, and my beliefs have always felt grounded in reality. It's really just my moods and energy levels that fluctuate so wildly.
Can you describe the severity of your energetic and irritable periods - have you ever had episodes where you didn't need sleep, spent excessively, or engaged in risky behaviors during those times?

During those high-energy phases, I feel an overflow of energy and can go for days with barely any sleep while still feeling completely refreshed and unbothered by it. However, I don't recall ever engaging in excessive spending or any risky behaviors during those times.
How long do these high-energy periods typically last, and have they ever required hospitalization or caused significant impairment in your social or occupational functioning?

These high-energy phases have been happening on and off for about a year and a month now. I have never needed to be hospitalized because of them, and although they make my life feel a bit chaotic, they haven't completely ruined my work or relationships.
I'm sorry, I think you might have gotten cut off there. What were you going to ask me next?

Have you ever had a high-energy period that was so severe it caused you to be hospitalized, or did you experience psychotic symptoms during any of those episodes, which would distinguish a more severe manic episode?
No, I have never been hospitalized during those high-energy periods. I also haven't experienced any psychotic symptoms, like hearing voices or seeing things, during those times.

Did these high-energy periods, although not severe enough to cause hospitalization, still significantly impact your daily life, relationships, or work, but perhaps in a less severe way than a full manic episode would?
I'm not quite sure how to measure the exact impact those periods have had on my life. I haven't really thought about it in that specific way, other than just feeling like things get a bit chaotic.
Can you think of any specific situations or instances where your high-energy periods may have affected your relationships, work performance, or daily routines, even if it was in a subtle way?

Yes, actually. I often start multiple projects at once and stay up all night working on them because I don't feel any need to sleep. At the same time, I get incredibly irritable and snap at people over minor things, which has definitely strained my relationships.

It sounds like these high-energy periods have had a noticeable impact on your life and relationships. To confirm, you've experienced periods of hypomania, characterized by increased energy, reduced need for sleep, and irritability, but not to the extent of causing significant impairment or hospitalization, correct?

Yes, that is completely accurate. I definitely experience those high-energy phases where I barely need to sleep and get very irritable, which is really intense and noticeable. However, it has never gotten to the point where I needed to be hospitalized or was completely unable to function.

Based on what you've shared, it seems that your symptoms align with the criteria for Bipolar II Disorder, which involves periods of hypomania and major depressive episodes. Is that a diagnosis that resonates with you, or would you like to discuss further?

That diagnosis actually makes a lot of sense to me, as I've spent the last year alternating between those intense, sleepless high-energy phases and long periods of deep sadness, emptiness, and loss of interest. It is honestly a relief to put a name to what I've been going through, and I would really like to discuss what our next steps are for managing it.
